chapters.summary: The logic, evidence, and verification method for True/False/Not Given and Yes/No/Not Given.

blocks.text: No question type frightens candidates more than this one, and the fear has a single source: Not Given. True and False feel manageable. Not Given feels like guessing. It is not. Not Given is a precise verdict with precise rules, and by the end of this masterclass you will reach it with the same confidence as the other two. The secret is that this is not really a reading task. It is a logic task. You are comparing a claim against evidence and naming the relationship between them. Master the logic and the type becomes one of the most reliable in the test.
THE THREE VERDICTS

Fix these definitions exactly. Most errors come from blurring them. TRUE. The passage confirms the statement. It states the same thing, or says it in different words with the same meaning. FALSE. The passage contradicts the statement. It says the opposite, or something that cannot both be true with the statement. NOT GIVEN. The passage neither confirms nor contradicts the statement. The information is absent or insufficient. The topic may even appear, but this specific claim is not settled by the text.

False means the passage says the opposite. Not Given means the passage does not say. These are completely different. Confusing “the passage disagrees” with “the passage is silent” is the deepest TFNG error, and it costs marks in both directions.
THE METHOD: CLAIM, EVIDENCE, RELATIONSHIP

Run these three steps on every statement, in order. Step 1: CLAIM. Read the statement and pin down exactly what it asserts. Break it into parts. What is the subject? What is being claimed about it? Are there any quantifiers (all, some, most), comparisons (more than, the largest), or qualifiers (only, always, sometimes)? Underline the precise words that carry the claim, because those exact words are what the evidence must match, contradict, or leave alone. Step 2: EVIDENCE. Locate the passage lines on the same subject. TFNG follows passage order, so move forward through the text. Read the relevant sentence and its neighbours carefully. This is close reading, not scanning.

Step 3: RELATIONSHIP. Decide how the evidence relates to the claim: - The evidence confirms the claim, in the same or paraphrased words: TRUE. - The evidence contradicts the claim: FALSE. - The evidence does not address the exact claim, or addresses only part of it: NOT GIVEN. Claim, evidence, relationship. Never skip to a verdict without naming the relationship. The verdict is the name of the relationship, nothing more.
THE DISTINCTIONS THAT DECIDE THE HARD ONES

The difficult items all turn on telling these five relationships apart. Contradiction (False). The passage states the opposite. This includes an opposite fact, a different number or date, a clashing quantifier (statement says “all,” passage says “some”), or a reversed comparison (statement says A beats B, passage says B beats A). Absence (Not Given). The passage simply does not address the claim. The topic may be present, but this specific point is never made either way. Absence is Not Given, never False. Partial information (usually Not Given). The statement makes a compound claim, and the passage supports only part of it. For a statement to be True, every part must be supported. If one part is confirmed but another is never addressed, the whole statement is Not Given. If one part is contradicted, the whole statement is False. Inference and assumption (danger). You may accept a clear paraphrase or a meaning the passage necessarily carries. You may not accept something that is merely plausible, likely, or a reasonable guess. If you have to assume a fact the passage does not state in order to call the statement True, the honest verdict is Not Given. The line is: necessary meaning is allowed; probable-in-the-real-world is not. Outside knowledge (trap). Judge only by the passage, never by what you know about the world. A statement can be factually true in reality and still be Not Given, because the passage did not say it. Delete your own knowledge for this task.
PRACTICAL DECISION RULES

Carry these into the exam. • If the statement is stronger or more specific than the passage, it is usually False or Not Given. False if the passage contradicts it, Not Given if the passage simply never goes that far. • Extreme words (all, only, never, always, none, every) deserve suspicion. Passages rarely support absolutes, so a statement with an extreme word is often False or Not Given. Check whether the passage really makes the absolute claim. • Absence is Not Given, not False. If you cannot find the claim addressed at all, that is Not Given. Do not mark False just because you cannot confirm it.
• False needs a real contradiction. Before writing False, find the sentence that says the opposite. If you cannot point to it, you are probably looking at Not Given.

blocks.title: TUTOR INSIDER TIP
blocks.text: When you feel yourself thinking “well, that’s probably true” or “that would make sense,” stop. Probably and would-make-sense are the exact feelings that signal Not Given. True is for what the passage confirms, not for what seems reasonable. Your own agreement with a statement is not evidence.
blocks.bn: যখন মনে হয় “এটা তো সম্ভবত সত্যি” বা “এটা যুক্তিসঙ্গত”, তখনই থামুন। “সম্ভবত” আর “যুক্তিসঙ্গত” অনুভূ তিটাই Not Given-এর ইঙ্গিত। প্যাসেজ নিশ্চিত করলে True, আপনার মনে হলে নয়।

blocks.text: YES / NO / NOT GIVEN

Yes/No/Not Given uses the identical logic, with one change of target. TFNG tests facts and information. YNNG tests the writer’s views, claims, and opinions. • YES. The writer holds or asserts this view. • NO. The writer holds or asserts the opposite view. • NOT GIVEN. The writer’s view on this is not given. The extra skill is spotting where the writer’s opinion lives. Look for opinion language: argues, believes, suggests, claims, contends, clearly, surely, unfortunately, worryingly, rightly, it is a mistake to. Neutral fact-reporting is not the writer’s opinion; a sentence that simply states what happened tells you nothing about what the writer thinks. In YNNG, you are tracking the writer’s stance, so read for judgement words, not just facts.

EXPERT THINKING: a Not Given that looks True Statement: “The waggle dance took von Frisch many years to decode.” Passage: “The dance was first decoded by Karl von Frisch in the mid-twentieth century, work for which he later received a Nobel Prize.” WHAT A BEGINNER THINKS “Decoding something that complex must have taken years. That sounds right. True.” WHAT AN EXPERIENCED STUDENT THINKS “The passage talks about the decoding and von Frisch, so the answer is probably here. Leans True but feels unsure.” WHAT AN EXPERT CANDIDATE NOTICES The claim is specifically about how long it took. The passage says who decoded it and when, and that he won a prize, but says nothing about the duration of the work. The topic is present; this exact claim is absent. To call it True, you would have to assume the timescale, which is inference, not evidence. Verdict: Not Given. The plausibility was the trap. The lesson: a statement about a detail the passage never gives is Not Given, no matter how reasonable it sounds and no matter how much of its topic appears in the text.
PRACTICE: 27 ORIGINAL QUESTIONS
Three original passages. Apply claim, evidence, relationship to every statement, then check the reasoning. Do not just mark right or wrong; confirm you named the correct relationship.

PASSAGE A (for questions 1 to 10) Honeybees share the location of food through a behaviour known as the waggle dance. A returning forager runs in a figure-of-eight on the vertical honeycomb, waggling her abdomen during the straight central run. The angle of that run relative to vertical encodes the direction of the food relative to the sun, while the duration of the waggle indicates the distance: a longer waggle means a more distant source. The dance was first decoded by Karl von Frisch in the mid-twentieth century, work for which he later received a Nobel Prize. Other bees follow the dancer closely, and many fly out to the described location, though some ignore the dance entirely and forage where they please. The dance is less precise for very close food sources, for which bees use a simpler round dance instead. True / False / Not Given: 1. The waggle dance tells other bees where food can be found. 2. The direction of the food is shown by how long the bee waggles. 3. Karl von Frisch received a Nobel Prize for work on the dance. 4. Von Frisch decoded the dance in the nineteenth century. 5. Every bee that watches the dance flies to the food. 6. The round dance is used for food sources that are very far away. 7. The waggle dance is performed on a horizontal surface. 8. Von Frisch’s findings were initially rejected by other scientists. 9. Bees can also communicate the quality of a food source through the dance. 10. The dance is more precise for distant sources than for very close ones.

PASSAGE B (for questions 11 to 20) Recovered in 1901 from an ancient shipwreck off the Greek island of Antikythera, the corroded bronze device now known as the Antikythera mechanism has puzzled researchers for over a century. Roughly the size of a shoebox, it originally held at least thirty interlocking gears. Modern imaging has revealed that it modelled the movements of the sun and moon and could predict eclipses, functioning as a kind of astronomical calculator. Most scholars date its construction to the second century BCE. Nothing of comparable mechanical complexity is known from the following thousand years, which has led some to call it the first analogue computer. The identity of its maker remains unknown, though its sophistication suggests a long tradition of

similar instruments that have not survived. Replicas built from the imaging data confirm that the surviving gear ratios reproduce genuine astronomical cycles. True / False / Not Given: 11. The mechanism was found in the twentieth century. 12. The device contained fewer than twenty gears. 13. The mechanism could be used to predict eclipses. 14. The mechanism was considerably larger than a shoebox. 15. Most scholars agree on the identity of the mechanism’s maker. 16. Devices of similar complexity were common in the centuries that followed. 17. The mechanism was made of iron. 18. Replicas have shown that the gears reproduce real astronomical cycles. 19. Other astronomical instruments were found in the same shipwreck. 20. The mechanism took several years to construct.

PASSAGE C (for questions 21 to 27) Some argue that teaching handwriting is a waste of classroom time in an age of keyboards. I find this view short-sighted. The research I have seen suggests that forming letters by hand supports early reading and memory in ways typing does not, and to abandon it would be to trade a proven benefit for mere convenience. Of course, children must also learn to type; no one sensible disputes that. But the two are not in competition, and framing them as either-or is a false choice. What worries me is not that schools teach typing, but that some now teach nothing else. Handwriting need not dominate the timetable; a few minutes a day would preserve its benefits. The claim that handwriting harms children by slowing them down strikes me as unpersuasive. Yes / No / Not Given (the writer’s views): 21. The writer believes teaching handwriting wastes classroom time. 22. The writer thinks children should not learn to type. 23. The writer regards handwriting and typing as opposed alternatives. 24. The writer is concerned that some schools now teach only typing. 25. The writer believes handwriting improves children’s creativity. 26. The writer thinks handwriting should take up most of the timetable. 27. The writer finds the argument that handwriting slows children down convincing.
ANSWER KEY AND REASONING

Passage A 1. TRUE. Claim: the dance communicates food location. Evidence: “share the location of food through… the waggle dance.” Relationship: confirmed, paraphrased (“tells where food can be found” equals “share the location”).

2. FALSE. Claim: direction is shown by waggle duration. Evidence: angle encodes direction; duration indicates distance. Relationship: contradiction. Direction and distance are swapped. 3. TRUE. Evidence: “work for which he later received a Nobel Prize.” Confirmed. 4. FALSE. Claim: nineteenth century. Evidence: “mid-twentieth century.” Contradiction (wrong century). 5. FALSE. Claim: every watching bee flies to the food. Evidence: “some ignore the dance entirely.” Contradiction via quantifier: “every” versus “some ignore.” 6. FALSE. Claim: round dance for very far food. Evidence: round dance is for “very close food sources.” Contradiction. 7. FALSE. Claim: horizontal surface. Evidence: “vertical honeycomb.” Contradiction. 8. NOT GIVEN. Claim: findings were initially rejected. Evidence: the passage covers the decoding and the prize but says nothing about how other scientists received the work. Absence, so Not Given, not False. 9. NOT GIVEN. Claim: bees communicate food quality. Evidence: the passage covers location, direction, and distance, but never quality. Absence. Note the topic (what the dance communicates) is present, yet this specific claim is not, which is the classic Not Given shape. 10. TRUE. Claim: more precise for distant than very close sources. Evidence: “less precise for very close food sources.” Relationship: confirmed by necessary meaning. If it is less precise for very close sources, it is more precise for the rest, including distant ones. This is allowed paraphrase, not a leap. Passage B 11. TRUE. Evidence: “Recovered in 1901.” 1901 is the twentieth century. Confirmed. 12. FALSE. Claim: fewer than twenty gears. Evidence: “at least thirty interlocking gears.” Contradiction (number clash). 13. TRUE. Evidence: “could predict eclipses.” Confirmed. 14. FALSE. Claim: considerably larger than a shoebox. Evidence: “roughly the size of a shoebox.” Contradiction. “Larger than” conflicts with “roughly the size of.” 15. FALSE. Claim: scholars agree on the maker’s identity. Evidence: “the identity of its maker remains unknown.” Contradiction. 16. FALSE. Claim: similar devices were common afterwards. Evidence: “nothing of comparable mechanical complexity is known from the following thousand years.” Contradiction. 17. FALSE. Claim: made of iron. Evidence: “bronze device.” Contradiction.

18. TRUE. Evidence: “Replicas… confirm that the surviving gear ratios reproduce genuine astronomical cycles.” Confirmed. 19. NOT GIVEN. Claim: other astronomical instruments in the same wreck. Evidence: the passage mentions the shipwreck but says nothing about other instruments in it. Absence. 20. NOT GIVEN. Claim: it took several years to build. Evidence: the passage never states the construction time. Absence. Plausible, but not stated, so Not Given, not True. Passage C (Yes / No / Not Given) 21. NO. The writer reports that “some argue” this, then says “I find this view short-sighted.” The writer’s own view is the opposite of the statement. 22. NO. Evidence: “children must also learn to type; no one sensible disputes that.” The writer supports typing, contradicting the claim that children should not learn it. 23. NO. Evidence: “the two are not in competition, and framing them as either-or is a false choice.” The writer rejects the opposed-alternatives view. 24. YES. Evidence: “What worries me is… that some now teach nothing else.” The writer does hold this concern. 25. NOT GIVEN. The writer credits handwriting with supporting “early reading and memory,” but says nothing about creativity. Absence, even though related benefits are discussed. 26. NO. Evidence: “Handwriting need not dominate the timetable.” The writer’s view is the opposite of the claim. 27. NO. Evidence: the slowing-down argument “strikes me as unpersuasive.” The writer does not find it convincing. The pattern to take away: every False came with a sentence you could point to that said the opposite. Every Not Given came from the passage being silent on the exact claim, even when the surrounding topic was present. No verdict rested on what seems reasonable. Claim, evidence, relationship, every time.

blocks.text: Two things in one file. First, Matching Headings, the type that most rewards reading for main idea rather than detail. Then the Reading Trap Library, a single reference gathering every trap in the module, so you can revise them in one place before the exam.
PART 10

THE MATCHING HEADINGS MASTERCLASS What it is and what it tests You are given a list of headings and asked to choose the correct heading for each paragraph or section. There are always more headings than paragraphs, so some headings are distractors that fit nothing.

Matching Headings tests one thing: can you identify the main idea, or the purpose, of a whole paragraph. It does not test details. A heading must capture what the entire paragraph is about, not one fact inside it. This is why the type feels different from the others. Everywhere else you hunt for a specific detail. Here you must step back and see the paragraph as a whole.

Why matching one keyword is never enough The commonest failure is to spot a heading’s word inside a paragraph and match on that. It fails for two reasons. First, a heading’s keyword may appear in a paragraph that is mainly about something else, so the word is there but the main idea is not. Second, the paragraph’s real point may be expressed in completely different words from the heading, because headings are paraphrases. Matching a single word ignores both problems. The correct unit of matching is the whole idea of the paragraph against the whole idea of the heading. One word is never the main idea.

How to find a paragraph’s main idea Ask one question of the paragraph: “What is this paragraph mainly doing, or mainly about?” Answer it in a few words, in your own words, before you look at the headings. Where the main idea sits varies: • Often in the first sentence (the topic sentence). • Sometimes in the last sentence, if the paragraph builds to its point. • Sometimes nowhere explicit, so you synthesise it from the whole paragraph.

Remember the principle from File 09: the first sentence shows the paragraph’s direction but is not always its full main idea. If the first sentence is a hook, an example, or background, read on to find the real point. Crucially, separate the main idea from the supporting material. A paragraph may contain an example, a statistic, a contrast, or a minor detail, and none of these is the main idea; they serve it. The heading must match the point the paragraph is making, not the example it uses to make it.

Name the paragraph’s purpose It helps to name what job the paragraph does. Common purposes: • giving background or context • presenting a problem • offering a solution • describing a cause • describing an effect or result • giving an example • making an argument or a claim • reporting a research finding • drawing a contrast • summarising or concluding When you can say “this paragraph presents a problem” or “this paragraph reports a finding,” the right heading usually becomes obvious, because good headings often describe exactly these purposes.

The method, step by step 1. Read the paragraph, leaning on the topic sentence but checking the arc of the whole. 2. In your own words, state its main idea or purpose in a few words. Do this before reading the headings, so the headings cannot bias you. 3. Find the heading that matches your summary. 4. Check that no other paragraph fits that heading better, since each heading is used once. 5. Cross off used headings, and remember the leftover headings are distractors that were never meant to fit. Do the paragraphs you are confident about first, and cross off their headings, which narrows the choices for the harder paragraphs. If an example paragraph comes already matched in the instructions, use it: it removes one heading and shows you the level of paraphrase to expect.

Heading-specific traps • A heading that matches a detail or example in the paragraph rather than its main idea. • Two similar headings that differ by one important word; only one fits, so read both fully.
• A heading that matches the first sentence when that sentence was only a lead-in, not the paragraph’s point.

Beginner versus expert Beginner: reads the headings first, then hunts each heading’s keyword in the paragraphs, matching on words. Expert: reads each paragraph first, summarises its main idea in their own words, then finds the heading that fits the summary, immune to keyword bait.

Worked example Passage (practice): Paragraph A. Trees in cities do far more than decorate. They cool streets by casting shade and releasing water vapour, filter pollutants from the air, absorb rainfall that would otherwise flood drains, and have been linked to lower stress in residents. A single mature street tree can provide benefits worth many times the cost of planting it. Paragraph B. Yet urban trees lead hard lives. Compacted soil starves their roots of air and water, road salt poisons them, and construction severs roots without warning. A newly planted city tree often survives only a fraction of the lifespan it would reach in a forest, and many die within a decade. Paragraph C. Cities are now rethinking how they plant. Rather than squeezing trees into narrow pits, some use large shared soil trenches beneath the pavement, giving roots room to spread. Choosing species suited to local conditions, and watering them through their first summers, dramatically improves survival. Paragraph D. Recent studies add urgency. Researchers tracking city temperatures found that well-shaded streets can be several degrees cooler than bare ones during heatwaves, a gap expected to widen as the climate warms. Today’s saplings are tomorrow’s cooling infrastructure. Headings: i. The many benefits trees bring to cities ii. Why city trees struggle to survive iii. New ways of planting for longer life iv. Evidence that trees help cities cope with heat v. The cost of removing mature trees vi. How trees are planted in forests vii. The benefits of trees in the countryside Summaries in your own words: A is “the good things trees do for cities,” B is “why city trees die,” C is “better ways to plant them,” D is “research showing trees cool cities.” Matches: A to i, B to ii, C to iii, D to iv. The distractors teach the traps. Heading vii (“benefits… in the countryside”) is a similar- heading trap for i: same idea of benefits, wrong location, since paragraph A is about cities. Heading v (removing trees) and vi (forests) match single words that appear in the passage (“mature,” “forest”) but not any paragraph’s main idea. A keyword-matcher is pulled towards them; a main-idea reader is not.

PART 11

THE READING TRAP LIBRARY Here, in one place, are the traps that cost the most marks in Reading. Several appeared in earlier files; this is your consolidated revision reference. For each: what it looks like, why students fall, how to recognise it, how to avoid it, and an example.

Trap 1: Identical words, wrong meaning Looks like: a question and a passage sentence share a distinctive word, but the sentences mean different things. Why students fall: a matching word feels like a found answer, so they stop reading. Recognise it: you chose an answer mainly because a word matched. Avoid it: match meaning, not words; read the whole sentence around the shared word. Example: the question mentions “Mediterranean” and so does the passage, but the passage says “western Mediterranean” while the question says “whole Mediterranean.” (Fuller treatment: File 10.)

Trap 2: Right information, wrong paragraph Looks like: the correct-sounding information appears, but in a paragraph that does not answer this question. Why students fall: they grab the first place the topic appears. Recognise it: you answered from a different region than the question points to. Avoid it: use question order and the question’s exact subject to confirm you are in the right paragraph. Example: a detail about cost appears in paragraph two, but the question’s cost claim is settled in paragraph four.

Trap 3: Partial truth Looks like: part of a statement is supported, part is not, or part is contradicted. Why students fall: they see the supported part and stop, marking True. Recognise it: the statement has two or more parts joined together. Avoid it: require every part to be supported for True. One unsupported part means Not Given; one contradicted part means False. Example: “The device had thirty gears and was made of iron.” Thirty gears is supported; iron is contradicted (bronze). The whole is False. (See File 13.)

Trap 4: Extreme wording Looks like: a statement uses an absolute (all, only, never, always, none) that the passage does not support. Why students fall: they match the topic and ignore the strength of the claim. Recognise it: the statement contains an absolute word. Avoid it: check whether the passage really makes the absolute claim; it usually does not, making the statement False or Not Given. Example: “Every bee that watches the dance flies to the food,” when the passage says some ignore it. False. (See File 13.)

Trap 5: Examples mistaken for main ideas Looks like: a heading or answer matches an example the paragraph uses, not the point the paragraph makes. Why students fall: the example is concrete and memorable, more so than the abstract main idea. Recognise it: the thing you matched is introduced by “for example,” “such as,” “for instance,” or is one item among several. Avoid it: separate the main idea from its supporting examples; match the main idea. Example: a paragraph arguing that city trees face many threats uses “road salt” as one example; a heading about road salt would be a trap. (See Part 10 above.)

Trap 6: Inference Looks like: a statement that is not stated but seems to follow from the passage. Why students fall: they reason one step beyond the text and call it True. Recognise it: you had to add a thought the passage did not state. Avoid it: accept necessary meaning and clear paraphrase, but not probable-sounding conclusions. If you inferred it, it is Not Given. Example: “Decoding the dance took von Frisch years,” when the passage never gives the duration. Not Given. (See File 13.)

Trap 7: Outside knowledge Looks like: a statement that is true in the real world but not stated in the passage. Why students fall: they answer from what they know rather than what they read. Recognise it: you know it is true but cannot find it in the text. Avoid it: judge only by the passage; delete your own knowledge for this task. Example: “Bees are important pollinators” is true in life, but if the passage does not say it, the verdict is Not Given.

Trap 8: Similar headings Looks like: two headings that are almost the same, differing by one important word. Why students fall: they pick the first that looks close and move on. Recognise it: two headings share most of their words. Avoid it: read both fully and find the word that distinguishes them, then match that word to the paragraph’s actual point. Example: “benefits of trees in cities” versus “benefits of trees in the countryside.” (See Part 10 above.)

Trap 9: Numerical traps Looks like: a number in the statement differs from, or is reworded from, the passage figure. Why students fall: they match the presence of a number without checking its value or what it refers to. Recognise it: the statement contains a figure, fraction, or proportion. Avoid it: check the exact value and what it counts. “At least thirty” contradicts “fewer than twenty”; “half” equals “fifty per cent.” Example: “The device had fewer than twenty gears,” when the passage says at least thirty. False. (See File 13.)

Trap 10: Comparison traps Looks like: a comparison is reversed, or a mere comparison is inflated into a superlative. Why students fall: they check that a comparison exists without checking its direction or strength. Recognise it: the statement contains “more than,” “less than,” “the most,” “the largest,” “faster than.” Avoid it: confirm which item is greater, and whether the claim is “more than some” or

“more than all.” Reversed direction means False; comparative inflated to superlative usually means Not Given. Example: “The region produces more cork than all other countries combined,” when the passage says only “more than any other single country.” Not Given. (Full treatment: File 10.)
PRACTICE: TRAP SPOTTING

For each item, give the verdict and name the trap it is built on. Use the urban trees passage above. Reasoning keys follow. 1. (TFNG) “Road salt is the main reason city trees die.” 2. (TFNG) “City trees never reach the lifespan they would in a forest.” 3. (TFNG) “Well-shaded streets can be cooler than bare streets in hot weather.” 4. (TFNG) “Trees improve residents’ mental health more than they reduce flooding.” 5. (Heading) A student matches Paragraph C to the heading “The problem of compacted soil.” Which trap is this?
ANSWER KEY AND REASONING

1. NOT GIVEN. Trap: examples mistaken for main ideas (and extreme wording). The passage lists road salt as one of several threats (“compacted soil… road salt… construction”), never as “the main reason.” Treating one example as the whole point, plus the unsupported “main,” makes this unsupported. Not Given. 2. NOT GIVEN. Trap: extreme wording. The passage says a city tree “often survives only a fraction” of its forest lifespan, and “many die within a decade.” “Often” and “many” are not “never.” The absolute “never reach” goes beyond what the passage supports. (It is not False, because the passage does not say they do reach it either; it is simply not the claim made.) 3. TRUE. Verify against: “well-shaded streets can be several degrees cooler than bare ones during heatwaves.” Confirmed, paraphrased (“hot weather” for “heatwaves”). No trap; a straight match. Included so you do not start seeing traps everywhere; some statements are simply True. 4. NOT GIVEN. Trap: comparison / inference. The passage says trees are “linked to lower stress” and that they “absorb rainfall,” but it never compares the size of these two benefits. The comparison “more than” is invented. Not Given. 5. Trap: right information, wrong paragraph (and example-as-main-idea). Compacted soil is mentioned, but in Paragraph B (the threats), not Paragraph C. Paragraph C’s main idea is better planting methods. The student matched a detail from the wrong paragraph. The correct heading for C is “New ways of planting for longer life.”

The lesson of the whole library: nearly every Reading trap is a version of one mistake, matching a word, a part, or a topic instead of the whole, exact meaning. Verify meaning, check every part, confirm the location, and watch the small words, and the traps stop working.

blocks.text: You now have every reading skill and every question type. This final file turns them into a plan for the sixty minutes themselves, tuned to your target band, and then gives you a timed capstone to run it on.
PART 12
THE 60-MINUTE READING BATTLE PLAN Three passages, forty questions, sixty minutes, no extra time. That is roughly twenty minutes per passage including its questions. The plan below wins that fight.

The universal rules (every band obeys these) 1. Never read the whole passage first. Skim to build a paragraph map (two to three minutes), then let the questions drive. Reading everything is the single biggest time sink. 2. Secure the cheap marks first. Passage 1 is easiest and its marks are worth exactly as much as Passage 3’s. Get them before the clock tightens. 3. Keep a per-question budget. If a question resists after a fair look, mark your best guess, flag it, and move on. One question is one mark; three unreached questions are three marks. 4. Never leave a blank. No penalty for wrong answers, so every blank is a wasted chance. Fill all gaps before time ends, even with a guess. 5. Verify, do not agonise. Back each answer with evidence, then move. Confidence comes from evidence, not from re-reading.
The default time split, and how to bend it A clean default is twenty minutes per passage. Because difficulty rises, many candidates use a graduated split instead:

Passage Time Why Passage 1 about 17 minutes easiest, so bank time here Passage 2 about 20 minutes medium Passage 3 about 20 minutes hardest, but capped so it cannot swallow the test Check about 3 minutes fill blanks, review flags
The cap on Passage 3 is the point. A hard passage will happily eat forty minutes if you let it. Give it its share and no more.

Band-specific plans Targeting Band 5 (roughly 23 to 26 correct). Do not try to answer everything perfectly. Your marks live in Passage 1 and in the easier question types across all three passages: completion, short answer, and factual True/False. Do those thoroughly. Give the hardest types (some Matching Headings, Matching Information) a quick attempt, then guess and flag rather than grinding. Spend a little longer on Passages 1 and 2 where marks are reachable, and accept that some Passage 3 marks will be guesses. Goal: harvest every cheap mark, lose only the expensive ones. Targeting Band 6 (roughly 27 to 29). Do Passages 1 and 2 solidly, then give Passage 3 the time that remains. Attempt every question, but never get stuck: within a passage, skip a hard question and return after the easier ones. Use question order to move forward. Guarantee no blanks. Your lost marks should be a handful of genuine traps, not questions you never reached. Targeting Band 7 (roughly 30 to 32). Run a tight 17/20/20 split with a 3-minute check. Skim efficiently, get every easy and medium question right, and on Passage 3 lean on question order, elimination, and evidence. The marks you are fighting for now are traps and Not Givens, so verify every answer you are unsure of. Leave time to revisit flagged questions once. Targeting Band 8 and above (35 or more). You are fighting for near-perfection, and the entire battle is traps, Not Givens, and fine distinctions. Budget about 17/19/21 with a firm 3- minute check. You can afford to miss around five, so do not let one or two genuinely impossible items rattle you. Every answer must be evidence-backed; the difference between Band 7 and Band 8 is ruthless verification and never falling for the partial-truth or comparison traps.

Skipping and returning Flag any question you cannot settle within its budget. Do not carry its weight into the next question; a clean mind answers better than an anxious one. Return to flagged questions only after finishing the passage, and to the hardest ones only in the final check. Skipping is not failure; it is how you protect the marks you can still earn.

Prioritisation: order of attack within a passage 1. Do the ordered types top to bottom (TFNG, completion, sentence completion), letting each answer narrow the search. 2. Do Matching Information and Matching Headings after these, when you already know the passage. 3. Within any set, do the questions you can locate quickly first, and flag the stubborn ones for a second pass.
Difficult questions When a question resists: eliminate the options you can, then guess from what remains. For a stuck True/False/Not Given item, remember that if you cannot find a confirming or
contradicting sentence, the answer is probably Not Given. Do not spend a fourth minute; a reasoned guess plus a flag is the correct trade.

Final checking (the last 3 minutes) • Fill every blank with your best guess. • Revisit flagged questions once, briefly. • On completion answers, check the word limit and spelling. • Do NOT second-guess answers you backed with evidence. Changing an evidence-based answer under time pressure usually makes it worse. Trust the verification you already did.

blocks.title: TUTOR INSIDER TIP
blocks.text: Most candidates lose Reading marks not to hard questions but to the clock, by over- reading Passage 1 and starving Passage 3. If you fix only one thing, fix your pacing: set a hard limit for each passage and obey it even mid-question. A flagged guess in Passage 3 beats a perfect Passage 1 you spent twenty-eight minutes on.

blocks.text: PART 13

READING PRACTICE The whole module has drilled skills in isolation. Now assemble them. Below is a timed capstone: one passage with a mixed question set, exactly as a real passage mixes types. Give yourself twenty minutes. Skim first, then run the battle plan. For a full test, use three passages of real audio-free official material back to back in sixty minutes, because stamina across three passages is itself a skill. This single passage builds the machinery; the full test rehearses the endurance. Passage (practice, original): Few animals disguise themselves as completely as the octopus. In under a second it can change the colour, pattern, and even the texture of its skin to melt into a reef or a patch of sand. This ability serves two ends at once: hiding from predators, and communicating with other octopuses. The mechanism is layered. Just beneath the surface sit thousands of tiny sacs of pigment called chromatophores, each ringed by muscles; when the muscles pull, the sac spreads and its colour shows. Below these lie reflecting cells that scatter and bounce light, adding blues, greens, and silvers that the pigments alone cannot make. The skin can also raise small bumps, known as papillae, to imitate the rough texture of rock or coral. A puzzle remains at the heart of this skill. Octopuses appear to be colourblind: their eyes contain only one kind of light-detecting cell, which should make distinguishing colours impossible. Yet they match the colours of their surroundings with startling accuracy. One leading hypothesis is that the skin itself senses light, using the same light-sensitive proteins found in eyes, allowing the animal to “see” colour through its body. Beyond

camouflage, researchers study these displays for other reasons. The same skin is used in courtship and threat, flashing patterns that other octopuses read as signals. Engineers, meanwhile, look to octopus skin as a model for soft, colour-changing materials, hoping to build surfaces that adapt the way living skin does.

Questions Matching Headings. Choose a heading for paragraphs 2 and 3 from: i. A contradiction scientists cannot yet explain ii. How the colour change is produced iii. The dangers octopuses face iv. Why octopuses live alone 1. Paragraph 2 2. Paragraph 3 True / False / Not Given. 3. The octopus can change its skin texture as well as its colour. 4. Octopuses have several types of light-detecting cell in their eyes. 5. Octopuses use camouflage mainly to catch prey. Summary completion (ONE WORD from the passage). 6. Colour is produced by pigment sacs called ____, each surrounded by muscles. 7. To copy rough surfaces, the skin raises small bumps called ____. Multiple choice. 8. According to the passage, the reflecting cells beneath the chromatophores: A) produce the pigments, B) add colours the pigments cannot make, C) control the muscles. 9. The “puzzle” the passage describes is that octopuses: A) cannot change colour quickly, B) match colours despite appearing colourblind, C) have no predators. Matching Information. 10. Which paragraph mentions a possible use of octopus skin in engineering?
ANSWER KEY AND REASONING

1. ii. Paragraph 2’s main idea is how the colour change works (chromatophores, reflecting cells, papillae). Not a detail; the whole paragraph explains the mechanism. 2. i. Paragraph 3 presents the contradiction: colourblind eyes yet accurate colour- matching, with a hypothesis but no settled answer. “A contradiction scientists cannot yet explain” captures the purpose. Heading iii and iv match single ideas or nothing; they are distractors. 3. TRUE. Evidence: “change the colour, pattern, and even the texture.” Confirmed. 4. FALSE. Claim: several types of light-detecting cell. Evidence: “only one kind of light- detecting cell.” Contradiction (number clash). 5. NOT GIVEN. Claim: camouflage is used mainly to catch prey. Evidence: the passage says camouflage serves “hiding from predators, and communicating,” and later mentions hunting-related signalling, but never ranks catching prey as the main purpose. The “mainly” is unsupported. Absence plus extreme wording, so Not Given, not True or False.

6. chromatophores. Words-from-passage: “sacs of pigment called chromatophores, each ringed by muscles.” 7. papillae. “raise small bumps, known as papillae.” 8. B. Evidence: reflecting cells “add blues, greens, and silvers that the pigments alone cannot make.” A and C are contradicted or unsupported. 9. B. Evidence: “appear to be colourblind… Yet they match the colours… with startling accuracy.” The puzzle is exactly this contradiction. 10. Paragraph 4. “Engineers… look to octopus skin as a model for soft, colour-changing materials.” Matching Information wants the specific detail’s location, which is the final paragraph. Score yourself, then log. If you missed 5, note it as the classic partial-truth plus extreme- wording trap (the word “mainly”). If you missed a heading, you likely matched a detail rather than the paragraph’s whole purpose. Whatever you missed, write the reason code, not just the mark.
MODULE 2 WRAP-UP: READING IN ONE BREATH

Compressed to its core, Reading is this: Skim each passage in two to three minutes to build a paragraph map, never reading it all. Let the questions drive: for each, locate the region by scanning for anchors or paraphrased concepts, then close-read the few lines to identify and verify the answer. Match meaning, never a bare word. On True/False/Not Given, name the relationship between claim and evidence, and remember that silence is Not Given, not False. Watch the small words: all, only, might, more than. Guard your clock ferociously, secure the cheap marks first, skip and flag the stubborn ones, never leave a blank, and in the final check trust the answers you backed with evidence. That is the whole module. Not “read carefully,” but a precise sequence of locating, verifying, and deciding, run against the clock. When you can do it without thinking, the passage stops being a wall of text and becomes what it always was: a place where every answer is hidden in plain sight, waiting for a reader who knows exactly where to look. You should now be able to say, of any passage and any question type: “I know where to look and how to verify.” Two modules down. Turn next to Module 3, Writing, where the task changes completely: now you are not finding the answer, you are building it.
